replayr

replayr imports emulator recordings into R. It reads the buttons, keys, analogue sticks, pointer movement, touch, and motion-sensor values recorded during play, together with their timing and emulator metadata.

Getting started

Install from a source checkout:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_local("path/to/replayr")

Read a recording and extract one controller:

library(replayr)

path <- system.file("extdata", "sample.fm2", package = "replayr")
movie <- read_movie(path)
input <- player(movie, 1L)

n_frames(movie)
press_counts(movie)
button_layout(movie)

input is a logical matrix: rows are observations, columns are controls, and TRUE means active. button_layout() identifies each column. For another recording, pass its path to read_movie(); the file extension selects the reader. movie_members() lists recordings inside a ZIP download, and read_movie(path, member = ...) selects one of them.

Controllers and control identities

Each S3 object contains digital inputs, numeric channels, commands, and metadata. A replayr_movie stores its digital input in an array indexed by observation, controller, and control. Event-based formats retain the key and device fields present in the events; fixed gamepad layouts include unused buttons as well as pressed ones.

Columns are compact within each recording. Stable IDs and keys identify controls across layouts: a stick click, a direction derived from that stick, and an N64 C-button each have their own identity. button_layout(movie) gives the column-to-control mapping; button_layout() lists the shared registry. Keyboard identities retain the source convention, such as X KeySyms or Windows virtual keys.

The registry contains 53 consecutive IDs. Buttons with comparable roles share an ID across devices. The main mappings are:

Source controls Shared control and ID
Arcade Attack, Punch, or button 1; Doom Attack A (8)
Arcade buttons 5–8 L1, R1, L2, R2 (11–14)
Arcade D or button 4 Y (10)
Arcade Jump, Jump/Start, or button 2; Doom Use; missile B (7)
Arcade Kick or button 3 X (9)
GunCon trigger, side A, side B, and offscreen shot A, B, X, Y (8, 7, 9, 10)
Intellivision Top X (9)
Joystick buttons 1–8 A, B, X, Y, L1, R1, L2, R2 (8, 7, 9–14)
Keypad Clear and Enter Select (6) and Start (5)
Keypad digits 0–9 and Power Pad sensors 1–12 Equal numbers share numbered_0–numbered_12 (40–52)
Mouse buttons 4 and 5 L1 and R1 (11 and 12)
Mouse left, right, and middle buttons A, B, X (8, 7, 9)
Neo Geo A, B, C, and D A, B, X, Y (8, 7, 9, 10)
Super Scope trigger, cursor, turbo, and pause A, B, Mode, Start (8, 7, 19, 5)
View change Select (6)
Wii Remote 1/2, +/−, and Home X/Y (9/10), Start/Select (5/6), and Mode (19)

Wii Remote D-pad and A/B buttons use the gamepad IDs. Nunchuk C/Z use 17/18, Classic Controller buttons use the corresponding gamepad IDs, and libTAS Guide uses Mode. The microphone uses ID 53. Genesis and Saturn C retain ID 17 because those controllers have separate C and X buttons.

These mappings align controller roles; the action performed by a button still depends on the game. Keyboard keys, keypad Star/Pound, and controls without a defined counterpart retain qualified source IDs. For example, an arcade D button uses Y (10), while a libTAS keyboard D keeps control:keysym_64. openMSX device-qualified controls also remain separate, because its recordings can combine several devices in one input stream.

When multiple source buttons share an ID, the column is active if either is pressed. source_inputs and source_layout preserve the separate states and their mapping whenever aliases are combined. Wii device states also appear in poll_fields as wii_remote_* and wii_classic_* columns, which polls() includes for unassigned streams.

Universal button IDs for gamepads, both sticks, keypads, and peripherals, with named controls and numeric channels
aligned <- align_buttons(list(movie1, movie2))

The aligned matrices have matching columns, with absent controls filled by FALSE. Comparing game actions also requires a mapping from controls to their in-game meanings, such as Jump or Attack.

Analogue and positional input

analog_channels() returns recorded numeric values. By default, analog = "raw" leaves stick coordinates in this form. Four options add directions or angles: cardinal4, cardinal8, angle, and angle+magnitude. Settings can be chosen independently for each stick:

path <- system.file("extdata", "sample.dtm", package = "replayr")
movie <- read_movie(path,
  analog = c(left = "angle+magnitude", right = "cardinal8"))
head(analog_channels(movie))
head(stick_channels(movie))

Cardinal modes add logical direction columns. Angles increase counterclockwise from right: 0 degrees right, 90 up, 180 left, and 270 down. deadzone sets the radial threshold for an active direction. Magnitude measures displacement after applying the controller’s centre and scale; diagonal values can exceed one. The original coordinates remain available in every mode.

Mouse movement, light-gun aim, touch coordinates, dials, and motion sensors also appear in analog_channels(), with names and units determined by the recording format. Wii input can include accelerometer values, infrared points, and MotionPlus readings. Sensor calibration is needed to convert these counts to physical units. The package vignette demonstrates mouse dragging and Wii motion with original examples; open it with vignette("replayr", package = "replayr").

For BK2 recordings, system_channels() returns cabinet and emulator controls, such as coins, reset, disk selection, and input timing.

Timing and multiple controllers

Rows may represent video frames, controller polls, or timestamped events. n_frames() counts imported observations. The reader documentation describes the observation unit and any timing information stored in the file. LSMV also records input changes within video frames; movie$subframes identifies each observation’s frame and position.

M64 and DTM can contain multiple controllers without identifying the source port of each poll. These recordings return a replayr_poll_stream:

path <- system.file("extdata", "paper", "unassigned.dtm", package = "replayr")
stream <- read_dtm(path)
polls(stream)

The polls retain their source order. A controller_order established from the emulator can assign them to players. Wii and 3DS formats also distinguish reports from different devices; their observation flags identify which input fields each report supplies. See ?read_dtm and ?read_ctm for these fields.

Formats and platforms

The package reads 34 format families, with HGM as an alias for Hourglass WTF. The compatibility catalogue describes their versions, controller variants, and platform coverage.

Arcade FBM recordings require a game identifier or input_schema, since their fields follow the game driver’s order. Decoding legacy Wii extension controls requires the extension type and, when encrypted, its key. Reader help pages describe the arguments needed for each variant.

Large recordings

For BK2 logs that are too large to hold in memory, use a callback on successive chunks:

counts <- read_bk2_chunks("long-recording.bk2", press_counts)
Reduce(`+`, counts)

The input log is checked and extracted once. Temporary disk space must hold the expanded log; the callback determines how much output is retained. read_bk2() and read_lsmv() limit full imports to 256 MiB of expanded input by default. max_input_bytes can raise this limit when memory permits.

Tests and examples

The package includes original artificial recordings and their generators. They exercise individual controls, movement patterns, device combinations, and malformed input. Run the tests with devtools::test("path/to/replayr"). Optional external tests use separately obtained TASVideos recordings through REPLAYR_FIXTURE_DIR.
